NextItNet’s foundation is residual, causal dilated convolution for capturing short- and long-range item dependencies ([original paper](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf)). The closest recent convolutional result found is [TimeWeaver (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-8954/13/10/857): jointly learned temporal streams for different timescales, convolutional interactions, and temporal-feature calibration of positional encoding. It supports exploring time-sensitive convolutional representations, but does not establish that elapsed-time-conditioned NextItNet residual gates outperform item-conditioned gates. An older, directly relevant mechanism is [TLSRec (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04760), whose dimension-wise neural time gate adjusts long- versus short-term preferences using the lag since the last interaction.

A plausible adaptation—an experimental hypothesis—is to retain NextItNet’s causal dilated backbone and gate each residual update using the current hidden representation plus an embedding of log-scaled historical interaction gaps. Compare item-only, time-only, and joint gates within one independently trained network per category. Use only timestamps available in the observed prefix; TLSRec’s recommendation-time lag requires a query timestamp and must not be reconstructed from the held-out target. [FCSRec (IJCAI 2025)](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2025/389) cautions that poorly integrated temporal features can obstruct sequence dependencies. Temporal adaptation therefore warrants controlled validation; timestamps alone do not establish harmful stale interests or causal interest drift.
